newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian campaign violence hits Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian campaign violence hits Jakarta.

text.p: Supporters of Indonesia's ruling Golkar and a rival Moslem-oriented party clashed in several areas of Jakarta on Sunday as a second day of campaign violence ahead of May 29 elections hit the capital.
The city's police chief, Major-General Hamami Nata, said the situation was under control, but tension ran high across a southern swathe of the city.
Late on Sunday, the heads of the three political parties in the Jakarta area issued a statement cancelling mass outdoor rallies in the city for the remainder of the campaign.
They said that until the end of the campaign period on Friday, meetings would be confined to neighbourhood "dialogues" to avoid further violence and property damage.
But an official of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) told Reuters this did not necessarily mean people would not take to the streets again in already-illegal parades.
Backers of Golkar, the ruling party for the last 30 years, and its main PPP rival on Sunday hurled stones and other missiles at each other in at least five areas of the capital of 10 million people.

Witnesses said riot police and troops deployed in the city's southern Kebayoran Lama and Cipulir areas, in Otisea and Cawang in the east and in the central Proklamasi district to quell violence and keep the two sides apart.
Hamami said the situation was "still within the limits of tolerance", adding that the city was "relatively safe".
Another senior police officer on the scene ascribed at least some of the violence to rival communities with a tradition of confrontation and gang warfare which by chance had split along party lines.
The police chief reported no arrests or injuries and calm appeared to return to most areas after nightfall.

On Saturday, police used tear gas and rubber bullets and shot into the air to disperse thousands of PPP supporters in the Jati Negara district of eastern Jakarta who were protesting over being barred from a street previously open to Golkar.
The PPP has accused police of pro-Golkar bias.
Golkar, the PPP and the fractured Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only parties legally entitled to contest the general elections in which 125 million people are eligible to vote.
Golkar is expected to win easily after taking 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992.
The PPP is providing the main challenge after the Christian-Nationalist PDI was badly split when its leader was ousted by a government-backed faction last year.
Political analysts said support for the PPP also included a growing display of anti-government dissent, but added this would not affect the election outcome.
Witnesses said fighting in Kebayoran Lama started when a convoy of vehicles carrying Golkar supporters from a rally drove through an area heavily populated by PPP backers.
Golkar supporters in cars and riding motorcycles also drove into the other areas, challenging the local people to demonstrate support for the ruling party.
Almost all the violence so far during the official 23-day campaign period which started on April 27 has been between supporters of Golkar and the PPP, mainly in central Java.
An armed formes spokesman said that as of last Thursday, 73 people had died during the campaign, most in traffic accidents.
